## What the gate actually ran

`benchmarks/agent-brain` is Python, so `go test ./...` never sees it and `benchmark-corpus` is its only gate. It ran a fixed list of five scripts, two of them narrowed to one `TestCase` class:

```
python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_publication_safety.py
python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/mined-scale/check_manifest.py
python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_mined_scale_manifest.py
python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/run_test.py PostBrainSetupTests
python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_profile_brief.py BriefProfileCorpusTest
```

From the job log of a recent green run, that is `Ran 1` + `Ran 3` + `Ran 3` + `Ran 3` — **ten tests in ten seconds**.

Not run, anywhere:

- **36 of the 39** `test_*.py` modules in the tree, including all 30 under `confirmatory/` and `analysis/`, `test_packet_format_ab.py`, `test_packet_format_v2_ab.py`, `test_isolation_repairs.py`, `test_forbidden_artifact_scope.py`, `test_history_answer_scrub.py`, `test_cached_plugin_repo_key.py`.
- **310 of run_test.py's 313 tests** — only `PostBrainSetupTests` was named. The other 15 classes run only in `release-evidence`, which is `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`, i.e. after merge.
- `mise run check`, the documented local gate, ran none of them either.

## Why it matters now

Every in-flight harness fix carries its evidence as a **new test file** — a path a fixed list does not name. A gate that cannot see a new test cannot certify one, so those changes were reported green by a check that had not executed the thing that proves them.

## The change

`ci_tests.py` discovers every `test_*.py` and `*_test.py` under `benchmarks/agent-brain` and runs each in its own interpreter. A new test file is picked up with no CI edit — that is the property that closes the class.

Separate processes are required, not incidental: several modules load `run.py` or an analyzer by path under a fixed module name via `importlib`, and two directories each contain a `test_power_analysis.py`. A single `unittest discover` process collides on module names and silently drops modules, which is this hole again.

Also wired into `mise run check` as `test:benchmarks`, so the local gate and CI agree.

## Quarantine

Three modules are red on a clean checkout today. They are listed with the reason each is red, so the gap is visible instead of silent:

| module | why |
|---|---|
| `confirmatory/test_power_analysis.py` | `power-calibration-exploratory-v1.json` names `evidence/replay-lab-clean/panel-p01-clean-proof-claude-20260618T195058Z/records.ndjson`; that panel was replaced by `20260816T084152Z` and deleted. `build_report()` raises, 38 of its 23 tests error. |
| `confirmatory/test_check_protocol.py` | committed analyzer manifest disagrees with the sources it hashes (`analyzer files[3]: content hash mismatch`). |
| `confirmatory/test_development_task_symptom_review.py` | needs `confirmatory/development-relevance-queries-v1.json`, which is gitignored and generated locally, so it cannot run on a clean checkout. |

The first two are pre-registered statistical/attestation contracts; repointing them is the contract owner's call, not a test fix. A quarantined module that starts passing **fails** the run, so the list cannot outlive its reasons.

## Verification

- Full suite: 40 modules, 37 pass + 3 quarantined, `~55s`, exit 0. Three consecutive clean-`__pycache__` sweeps, identical result.
- Dropping a deliberately failing `test_*.py` into the tree: exit 1 (the old list would have ignored it).
- Making a quarantined module pass: exit 1 with `quarantined module now passes, remove it from QUARANTINE`.
- `run_test.py` alone: 313 tests, 10/10 consecutive clean runs.","headRefName":"audit/ci-runs-benchmark-tests","number":181,"state":"OPEN","title":"ci: run the benchmark test suite by discovery instead of a five-script list","url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/181"}

## Impact

`mcpPositiveInt` and `mcpNonNegativeInt` (`internal/cli/mcp.go:1378`, `:1396`) enforced a floor and nothing else — `typed <= float64(math.MaxInt)` is not a bound, it is a type check.

An MCP client is not a trusted peer in this design: the agent driving it carries repository text in its context that an untrusted checkout can influence, and a `tools/call` is one line of JSON.

The argument is not merely a result count. It reaches allocation sizing:

- `internal/cli/history_fts.go:581` — `out := make([]scoredHistoryRecord, 0, limit)`
- `internal/cli/doc_fts.go:199,204` — `LIMIT ?` with `limit*4`, and `make([]scoredDocRecord, 0, limit*4)`
- `internal/cli/retrieve.go:209,322` — the history arm scales the same value by 2 then 3 (with overflow guards, but no ceiling)

So `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000000}}` decides how many elements the server asks the runtime for. Depending on element size that is either a panic the request recovery turns into an opaque `-32603 internal error` (what I observed end to end), or an allocation request under the `makeslice` cap that the process attempts and does not survive. Either way an unauthenticated argument, not the server, picks the number.

`context_lines` on `brain_get_code_snippet` has the same shape — `semantic_graph.go:894` adds it to `record.EndLine`, and `math.MaxInt64` there overflows the sum negative.

## Repro

`internal/cli/mcp_int_bounds_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestMCPIntegerArgumentsAreCapped
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1e+09; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpNonNegativeInt accepted limit=1e+09
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1.099511627776e+12; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=2147483647; it sizes a slice capacity
--- FAIL: TestMCPToolCallRejectsOversizedLimit
    error = {"code":-32603,"message":"internal error handling \"tools/call\""}
```

That last line is the whole point: on `main` an oversized `limit` does not produce a validation error, it produces a recovered internal failure. After the fix it is a clean `-32000 limit must be an integer between 1 and 10000`.

## Fix

`mcpIntegerArgMax = 10000`, enforced in both decoders. Far above any useful result count, depth, offset or context window; far below the point where the value becomes an allocation problem.

Enforced in the decoders rather than declared as `"maximum"` in each `inputSchema` **on purpose**: the tool definitions are sent on every `tools/list` and their size is budgeted in tokens — `TestMCPBrainBriefToolDefinitionGolden` asserts an exact 747-byte definition and documents the tokenizer accounting for the whole `tools/list` payload. Adding a `maximum` to ~25 integer properties would spend that budget restating a bound the server must check itself regardless. `brain_get_conversation` and `brain_concepts`, which already declare real semantic maxima, keep them.

Two existing assertions in `mcp_test.go` move from `"limit must be an integer greater than zero"` to `"limit must be an integer between 1 and"`. The rejection behaviour they cover is unchanged; only the message is more accurate.

## Mutation

Restoring `math.MaxInt` in either decoder reproduces the failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli/` clean.", "headRefName": "audit/sec-mcp-int-bounds", "number": 117, "title": "fix(mcp): integer tool arguments have no upper bound, so a tool call chooses an allocation size"}

## The drift

`mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` reject any integer argument above `mcpIntegerArgMax` (10000) with a `-32000` tool error. The JSON schema declared a floor and **no ceiling** on 27 of the surface's 30 integer arguments.

So a schema-validating MCP client believed `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000}}` was a legal call, sent it, and learned the real bound by being refused at runtime. The declaration understated the contract the handler enforces. #117 added the cap; the schema was never told about it.

`brain_get` was the exception — its `context_before`/`context_after`/`limit` already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream validator enforces (`conversationContextMax`, `conversationOutlineMaxLimit`). Its `after_turn` did not, and is fixed here.

## Fix

`maximum` declared alongside `minimum` in the `integerArg`/`nonNegativeIntegerArg` helpers and on `brain_get`'s inline `after_turn` schema. No handler behaviour changes — this makes the declaration state what the handler already did.

## Tests that pin the two sides together

- **`TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces`** walks every integer argument on every tool and requires a declared `maximum` that is never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by calling `mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` at the boundary and one past it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream validator uses. A new integer argument that forgets its ceiling fails here.
- **`TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden`** pins the whole declared surface — every name, description, and schema — in `testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json`. There was no golden over the full tool-definition JSON; the three existing goldens cover one tool each, chosen for their token budget. This one exists because a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a silent edit to a name or a bound propagates into consumers that never see this repo. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1`.

## Cost, measured

The declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument: **+432 bytes on the `tools/list` result, 26,074 -> 26,506 (+1.7%)**.

The three per-tool byte budgets are re-measured (747->763, 810->826, 987->1003). Their **token** counts in those comments are the earlier measurement and are **not** re-measured here — the pinned o200k_base asset is deliberately not a test dependency, so I could not recompute them honestly rather than estimate.

## Verification

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the description half. Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement.

Both matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings, and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The description said, flatly: *"Includes current worktree content by default."*

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. The handler leaves `semanticWorktree` false (`refresh.go:327` reads it, `mcp.go` never sets it), so the semantic index that `semantic=true` rebuilds is built from **committed HEAD**. The refresh command's own `RunE` carries the comment explaining why: *"--worktree belongs to seed/docs. A dirty semantic snapshot must be an explicit `brain index --worktree` operation."*

So an agent calling `brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true)` — the exact combination the description discusses — was left believing its semantic index reflected uncommitted work. It did not.

This is the same drift that shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree` and was corrected in #141. The MCP tool string and the two docs paragraphs describing `brain_refresh` were not part of that fix; they are corrected here.

## 2. `brain_index_repository` claimed a refresh it refuses, and hid its gate

- **"Build or refresh"** — `runSemanticIndex` errors with `semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it` unless `force=true`. The default cannot refresh. (#118 flagged this and left it, on the grounds that the `force` argument's own text disambiguates. I disagree: the top-level description is what an agent reads to *choose* the tool, and "refresh" is the wrong verb at exactly that moment.)
- **Path scoping was undeclared.** The path is confined to the bound repository root unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set, and a relative path resolves against that root rather than the working directory. This was the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate inline — `brain_delete_project`, `brain_list_projects` and the workspace tools all do, after #133, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the knob from the surface it is already reading. It is documented in README and `docs/limits.md`, but not where the agent is looking.
- **`profile` asserted a closed list.** It claimed *"full, fast, or syntax-only"*. Nothing in this repo validates the value or knows the set — it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider subprocess, and the CLI flag help for the same field says *"e.g. full, syntax-only"*. I could not verify whether `fast` exists, so rather than pick a side I removed the authoritative framing and made the string say what the code actually does. Flagging the two help strings still disagreeing as a follow-up for whoever owns the provider contract.

## Tests that pin declaration to behaviour

`mcpRefreshOptions` is extracted from the `brain_refresh` case block with **no behaviour change**, purely so the claim can be pinned against the handler rather than against a comment.

- **`TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler`** asserts in one test that `worktree` reaches `seed.worktree`, that `semanticWorktree` stays false in the `worktree=true, semantic=true` combination, that the default really is `worktree=true`, and that the description says all of this. If `brain_refresh` ever does start indexing the worktree, the test fails and forces the description to move with it.
- **`TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPathScope`** drives `mcpResolveIndexPath` — absolute path contained, relative path joined onto the bound root, env gate lifting containment — beside the strings that describe it, and fails if the description drifts back to "Build or refresh" or drops the gate name.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. The handler leaves `semanticWorktree` false (`refresh.go:327` reads it, `mcp.go` never sets it), so the semantic index that `semantic=true` rebuilds is built from **committed HEAD**. The refresh command's own `RunE` carries the comment explaining why: *"--worktree belongs to seed/docs. A dirty semantic snapshot must be an explicit `brain index --worktree` operation."*

So an agent calling `brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true)` — the exact combination the description discusses — was left believing its semantic index reflected uncommitted work. It did not.

This is the same drift that shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree` and was corrected in #141. The MCP tool string and the two docs paragraphs describing `brain_refresh` were not part of that fix; they are corrected here.

## 2. `brain_index_repository` claimed a refresh it refuses, and hid its gate

- **"Build or refresh"** — `runSemanticIndex` errors with `semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it` unless `force=true`. The default cannot refresh. (#118 flagged this and left it, on the grounds that the `force` argument's own text disambiguates. I disagree: the top-level description is what an agent reads to *choose* the tool, and "refresh" is the wrong verb at exactly that moment.)
- **Path scoping was undeclared.** The path is confined to the bound repository root unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set, and a relative path resolves against that root rather than the working directory. This was the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate inline — `brain_delete_project`, `brain_list_projects` and the workspace tools all do, after #133, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the knob from the surface it is already reading. It is documented in README and `docs/limits.md`, but not where the agent is looking.
- **`profile` asserted a closed list.** It claimed *"full, fast, or syntax-only"*. Nothing in this repo validates the value or knows the set — it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider subprocess, and the CLI flag help for the same field says *"e.g. full, syntax-only"*. I could not verify whether `fast` exists, so rather than pick a side I removed the authoritative framing and made the string say what the code actually does. Flagging the two help strings still disagreeing as a follow-up for whoever owns the provider contract.

## Tests that pin declaration to behaviour

`mcpRefreshOptions` is extracted from the `brain_refresh` case block with **no behaviour change**, purely so the claim can be pinned against the handler rather than against a comment.

- **`TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler`** asserts in one test that `worktree` reaches `seed.worktree`, that `semanticWorktree` stays false in the `worktree=true, semantic=true` combination, that the default really is `worktree=true`, and that the description says all of this. If `brain_refresh` ever does start indexing the worktree, the test fails and forces the description to move with it.
- **`TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPathScope`** drives `mcpResolveIndexPath` — absolute path contained, relative path joined onto the bound root, env gate lifting containment — beside the strings that describe it, and fails if the description drifts back to "Build or refresh" or drops the gate name.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2. #118 compared each tool's declared schema against its handler and fixed three items; this is the adversarial re-check of the rows it marked "none", plus the drift #117 introduced.

## The drift

`mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` reject any integer argument above `mcpIntegerArgMax` (10000) with a `-32000` tool error. The JSON schema declared a floor and **no ceiling** on 27 of the surface's 30 integer arguments.

So a schema-validating MCP client believed `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000}}` was a legal call, sent it, and learned the real bound by being refused at runtime. The declaration understated the contract the handler enforces. #117 added the cap; the schema was never told about it.

`brain_get` was the exception — its `context_before`/`context_after`/`limit` already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream validator enforces (`conversationContextMax`, `conversationOutlineMaxLimit`). Its `after_turn` did not, and is fixed here.

## Fix

`maximum` declared alongside `minimum` in the `integerArg`/`nonNegativeIntegerArg` helpers and on `brain_get`'s inline `after_turn` schema. No handler behaviour changes — this makes the declaration state what the handler already did.

## Tests that pin the two sides together

- **`TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces`** walks every integer argument on every tool and requires a declared `maximum` that is never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by calling `mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` at the boundary and one past it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream validator uses. A new integer argument that forgets its ceiling fails here.
- **`TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden`** pins the whole declared surface — every name, description, and schema — in `testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json`. There was no golden over the full tool-definition JSON; the three existing goldens cover one tool each, chosen for their token budget. This one exists because a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a silent edit to a name or a bound propagates into consumers that never see this repo. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1`.

## Cost, measured

The declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument: **+432 bytes on the `tools/list` result, 26,074 -> 26,506 (+1.7%)**.

The three per-tool byte budgets are re-measured (747->763, 810->826, 987->1003). Their **token** counts in those comments are the earlier measurement and are **not** re-measured here — the pinned o200k_base asset is deliberately not a test dependency, so I could not recompute them honestly rather than estimate.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

{"baseRefName": "audit/mcp-contract-bounds", "body": "<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/78
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the description half. Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement.

Both matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings, and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The description said, flatly: *"Includes current worktree content by default."*

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. The handler leaves `semanticWorktree` false (`refresh.go:327` reads it, `mcp.go` never sets it), so the semantic index that `semantic=true` rebuilds is built from **committed HEAD**. The refresh command's own `RunE` carries the comment explaining why: *"--worktree belongs to seed/docs. A dirty semantic snapshot must be an explicit `brain index --worktree` operation."*

So an agent calling `brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true)` — the exact combination the description discusses — was left believing its semantic index reflected uncommitted work. It did not.

This is the same drift that shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree` and was corrected in #141. The MCP tool string and the two docs paragraphs describing `brain_refresh` were not part of that fix; they are corrected here.

## 2. `brain_index_repository` claimed a refresh it refuses, and hid its gate

- **"Build or refresh"** — `runSemanticIndex` errors with `semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it` unless `force=true`. The default cannot refresh. (#118 flagged this and left it, on the grounds that the `force` argument's own text disambiguates. I disagree: the top-level description is what an agent reads to *choose* the tool, and "refresh" is the wrong verb at exactly that moment.)
- **Path scoping was undeclared.** The path is confined to the bound repository root unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set, and a relative path resolves against that root rather than the working directory. This was the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate inline — `brain_delete_project`, `brain_list_projects` and the workspace tools all do, after #133, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the knob from the surface it is already reading. It is documented in README and `docs/limits.md`, but not where the agent is looking.
- **`profile` asserted a closed list.** It claimed *"full, fast, or syntax-only"*. Nothing in this repo validates the value or knows the set — it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider subprocess, and the CLI flag help for the same field says *"e.g. full, syntax-only"*. I could not verify whether `fast` exists, so rather than pick a side I removed the authoritative framing and made the string say what the code actually does. Flagging the two help strings still disagreeing as a follow-up for whoever owns the provider contract.

## Tests that pin declaration to behaviour

`mcpRefreshOptions` is extracted from the `brain_refresh` case block with **no behaviour change**, purely so the claim can be pinned against the handler rather than against a comment.

- **`TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler`** asserts in one test that `worktree` reaches `seed.worktree`, that `semanticWorktree` stays false in the `worktree=true, semantic=true` combination, that the default really is `worktree=true`, and that the description says all of this. If `brain_refresh` ever does start indexing the worktree, the test fails and forces the description to move with it.
- **`TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPathScope`** drives `mcpResolveIndexPath` — absolute path contained, relative path joined onto the bound root, env gate lifting containment — beside the strings that describe it, and fails if the description drifts back to "Build or refresh" or drops the gate name.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

## Cursor finding and fix

Entire identified that the declared `after_turn` ceiling prevents pagination after turn 10,000. The underlying regression originated in #117's shared integer decoder; #156 published the same ceiling.

- `d2ed72f6` in #117 separates the comparison-only turn cursor from allocation/work limits. `mcpTurnCursorMax` is 2,147,483,647, exactly representable by JSON numbers and native ints on supported 32/64-bit platforms. Result sizes retain the 10,000 ceiling.
- `209578fd` in #156 advertises that same cursor range and verifies both boundary acceptance and rejection above it. The full-surface fixture records the change.
- The MCP navigation test fails before the fix at cursor 10,001 and passes afterward. Additional tests verify real outline pagination above that cursor, rejection of negative/fractional/nonfinite/wrong-type/overflow inputs, and preservation of page-size limits.
- The fix was merged through all intermediate parents into #157; the native finding was resolved with commit and test evidence.
''';p.write_text(s)
PY","max_output_tokens":500}));

- **`brain_search_graph`'s `offset` and `brain_get_code_snippet`'s `context_lines`** declared `minimum: 1` in their JSON schema, but both handlers (`mcpNonNegativeInt`) accept and default to `0`. A schema-validating MCP client would wrongly refuse to send the default value. Fixed the schema (added a `nonNegativeIntegerArg` helper, `minimum: 0`) since the handler behavior is correct and long-standing; the declared contract was stale.
- **`brain_get_architecture`'s description** claimed "boundary counts", a field `semanticGraphSchemaReport`/`graphMetrics` has never returned. It dispatches to the exact same handler as `brain_get_graph_schema` (`runSemanticGraphSchema`), whose real metrics are hotspots, entry points, packages, and layers. Fixed the description to match actual output and made the alias explicit, consistent with how the other aliased tools (`brain_index_status`, `brain_search_code`, `brain_detect_changes`) document their aliasing.
- **`docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md`'s tool catalog** was missing `brain_entity_history` — registered in code and documented in `README.md`, but absent from the guide's "Available tools" list.

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2. #118 compared each tool's declared schema against its handler and fixed three items; this is the adversarial re-check of the rows it marked "none", plus the drift #117 introduced.

## The drift

`mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` reject any integer argument above `mcpIntegerArgMax` (10000) with a `-32000` tool error. The JSON schema declared a floor and **no ceiling** on 27 of the surface's 30 integer arguments.

So a schema-validating MCP client believed `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000}}` was a legal call, sent it, and learned the real bound by being refused at runtime. The declaration understated the contract the handler enforces. #117 added the cap; the schema was never told about it.

`brain_get` was the exception — its `context_before`/`context_after`/`limit` already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream validator enforces (`conversationContextMax`, `conversationOutlineMaxLimit`). Its `after_turn` did not, and is fixed here.

## Fix

`maximum` declared alongside `minimum` in the `integerArg`/`nonNegativeIntegerArg` helpers and on `brain_get`'s inline `after_turn` schema. No handler behaviour changes — this makes the declaration state what the handler already did.

## Tests that pin the two sides together

- **`TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces`** walks every integer argument on every tool and requires a declared `maximum` that is never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by calling `mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` at the boundary and one past it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream validator uses. A new integer argument that forgets its ceiling fails here.
- **`TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden`** pins the whole declared surface — every name, description, and schema — in `testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json`. There was no golden over the full tool-definition JSON; the three existing goldens cover one tool each, chosen for their token budget. This one exists because a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a silent edit to a name or a bound propagates into consumers that never see this repo. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1`.

## Cost, measured

The declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument: **+432 bytes on the `tools/list` result, 26,074 -> 26,506 (+1.7%)**.

The three per-tool byte budgets are re-measured (747->763, 810->826, 987->1003). Their **token** counts in those comments are the earlier measurement and are **not** re-measured here — the pinned o200k_base asset is deliberately not a test dependency, so I could not recompute them honestly rather than estimate.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the description half. Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement.

Both matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings, and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The description said, flatly: *"Includes current worktree content by default."*

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2. #118 compared each tool's declared schema against its handler and fixed three items; this is the adversarial re-check of the rows it marked "none", plus the drift #117 introduced.

## The drift

`mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` reject any integer argument above `mcpIntegerArgMax` (10000) with a `-32000` tool error. The JSON schema declared a floor and **no ceiling** on 27 of the surface's 30 integer arguments.

So a schema-validating MCP client believed `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000}}` was a legal call, sent it, and learned the real bound by being refused at runtime. The declaration understated the contract the handler enforces. #117 added the cap; the schema was never told about it.

`brain_get` was the exception — its `context_before`/`context_after`/`limit` already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream validator enforces (`conversationContextMax`, `conversationOutlineMaxLimit`). Its `after_turn` did not, and is fixed here.

## Fix

`maximum` declared alongside `minimum` in the `integerArg`/`nonNegativeIntegerArg` helpers and on `brain_get`'s inline `after_turn` schema. No handler behaviour changes — this makes the declaration state what the handler already did.

## Tests that pin the two sides together

- **`TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces`** walks every integer argument on every tool and requires a declared `maximum` that is never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by calling `mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` at the boundary and one past it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream validator uses. A new integer argument that forgets its ceiling fails here.
- **`TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden`** pins the whole declared surface — every name, description, and schema — in `testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json`. There was no golden over the full tool-definition JSON; the three existing goldens cover one tool each, chosen for their token budget. This one exists because a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a silent edit to a name or a bound propagates into consumers that never see this repo. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1`.

## Cost, measured

The declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument: **+432 bytes on the `tools/list` result, 26,074 -> 26,506 (+1.7%)**.

The three per-tool byte budgets are re-measured (747->763, 810->826, 987->1003). Their **token** counts in those comments are the earlier measurement and are **not** re-measured here — the pinned o200k_base asset is deliberately not a test dependency, so I could not recompute them honestly rather than estimate.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the description half. Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement.

Both matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings, and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The description said, flatly: *"Includes current worktree content by default."*

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. The handler leaves `semanticWorktree` false (`refresh.go:327` reads it, `mcp.go` never sets it), so the semantic index that `semantic=true` rebuilds is built from **committed HEAD**. The refresh command's own `RunE` carries the comment explaining why: *"--worktree belongs to seed/docs. A dirty semantic snapshot must be an explicit `brain index --worktree` operation."*

So an agent calling `brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true)` — the exact combination the description discusses — was left believing its semantic index reflected uncommitted work. It did not.

This is the same drift that shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree` and was corrected in #141. The MCP tool string and the two docs paragraphs describing `brain_refresh` were not part of that fix; they are corrected here.

## 2. `brain_index_repository` claimed a refresh it refuses, and hid its gate

- **"Build or refresh"** — `runSemanticIndex` errors with `semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it` unless `force=true`. The default cannot refresh. (#118 flagged this and left it, on the grounds that the `force` argument's own text disambiguates. I disagree: the top-level description is what an agent reads to *choose* the tool, and "refresh" is the wrong verb at exactly that moment.)
- **Path scoping was undeclared.** The path is confined to the bound repository root unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set, and a relative path resolves against that root rather than the working directory. This was the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate inline — `brain_delete_project`, `brain_list_projects` and the workspace tools all do, after #133, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the knob from the surface it is already reading. It is documented in README and `docs/limits.md`, but not where the agent is looking.
- **`profile` asserted a closed list.** It claimed *"full, fast, or syntax-only"*. Nothing in this repo validates the value or knows the set — it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider subprocess, and the CLI flag help for the same field says *"e.g. full, syntax-only"*. I could not verify whether `fast` exists, so rather than pick a side I removed the authoritative framing and made the string say what the code actually does. Flagging the two help strings still disagreeing as a follow-up for whoever owns the provider contract.

## Tests that pin declaration to behaviour

`mcpRefreshOptions` is extracted from the `brain_refresh` case block with **no behaviour change**, purely so the claim can be pinned against the handler rather than against a comment.

- **`TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler`** asserts in one test that `worktree` reaches `seed.worktree`, that `semanticWorktree` stays false in the `worktree=true, semantic=true` combination, that the default really is `worktree=true`, and that the description says all of this. If `brain_refresh` ever does start indexing the worktree, the test fails and forces the description to move with it.
- **`TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPathScope`** drives `mcpResolveIndexPath` — absolute path contained, relative path joined onto the bound root, env gate lifting containment — beside the strings that describe it, and fails if the description drifts back to "Build or refresh" or drops the gate name.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the error-contract half. One handler-side fix, independent of #156/#157 (different file, sibling branch off the same base).

## The drift

`inspectBoundarySpec` is shared by the `boundaries` CLI command (two call sites) and the `brain_boundaries` MCP tool. Its rejection message was written for the CLI:

```
--kind must be route, tool, or workflow
```

So an agent that sent `{"name":"brain_boundaries","arguments":{"kind":"controller"}}` was told to correct a **flag that does not exist on the surface it is calling**. Over MCP the argument is the JSON field `kind`, which the tool's own schema declares and `validateMCPToolArguments` validates by that name. An agent taking the error literally has nowhere to go.

#118 found this and left it as cosmetic. It is small, but it is the error contract of a tool an agent drives blind, and this surface is about to be wrapped — so the misleading string would propagate.

## Fix

The message names the accepted values without naming a flag, which reads correctly from both callers. The CLI still tells the user exactly which values are valid, and cobra supplies the flag context there.

Scope deliberately kept to the shared helper: `facts_read_cmd.go:424` has the same `--kind` phrasing but is CLI-only — no MCP tool exposes a facts kind argument — so it is correct as written and untouched.

## Test

`TestMCPBoundariesInvalidKindErrorNamesTheMCPArgument` drives a real `tools/call` and asserts on the JSON-RPC response, so it pins the message as the MCP caller actually receives it rather than as the helper returns it. It fails both if `--kind` comes back and if the accepted values stop being named.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestBoundar|TestInspect|TestAgentSurface|TestSemanticBoundar'` green (78 tests). No existing test asserted the old string. Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.", "headRefName": "audit/mcp-boundaries-kind-error", "number": 158, "state": "OPEN", "title": "fix(mcp): stop brain_boundaries telling an MCP caller to fix a CLI flag", "url": "https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/158"}

The cli only appends `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` when `paths.WorktreeRoot` succeeds (`plugin.go:172`), so a stdio server spawned with a non-repo CWD gets **zero** scoping. Reproduced on the branch:

```

```

Unbound is the case where scoping matters most; it should fail closed.

**2. The workspace gate checks a different field than the fan-out uses.** `mcpEnforceWorkspaceScope` validates `repo.LocalPathHint`, but `buildWorkspaceGraphPayload` (`workspace.go:750,757`) resolves the brain via `brainDirForKey(repo.RepoKey)` and never consults it. A manifest entry with a hint inside the bound root and a foreign `repo_key` passes the gate and reaches the foreign brain — it even takes the index lock there:

```
BYPASS: hint-inside-root + foreign repo_key reached the foreign brain: "repo_key":"gh/victim/other"
```

Scope on `RepoKey`, the thing the fan-out actually dereferences.

**3. The amended threat model overstates the result.** `docs/recall_threat_model.md` now says "No MCP argument reaches a filesystem path", but `brain_ingest_traces` (`mcp.go:921-931` -> `semantic_graph.go:983` `readRuntimeTraces`) still takes an unconstrained path. Only `mcpResolveIndexPath` (`mcp.go:719`) is contained.

**Breaks a legitimate topology.** A workspace of sibling checkouts — `devenv/cli` + `devenv/entiredb`, which is the only arrangement `brain_workspace_*` exists for — is refused for all three tools, since siblings are never inside the bound root. That five existing tests needed `t.Setenv` to keep passing is the signal. A per-member skip with a warning preserves the feature while keeping the guarantee.

**1. The cli only appends `ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT` when `paths.WorktreeRoot` succeeds (`plugin.go:172`), so a stdio server spawned with a non-repo CWD gets **zero** scoping. Reproduced on the branch:

```
BYPASS: unbound MCP server erased foreign brain .../repos/gh/victim/other   (brain_delete_project)
BYPASS: unbound list_projects enumerated foreign projects: gh/victim/other, gh/victim/second
```

Unbound is the case where scoping matters most; it should fail closed.

**2. The workspace gate checks a different field than the fan-out uses.** `mcpEnforceWorkspaceScope` validates `repo.LocalPathHint`, but `buildWorkspaceGraphPayload` (`workspace.go:750,757`) resolves the brain via `brainDirForKey(repo.RepoKey)` and never consults it. A manifest entry with a hint inside the bound root and a foreign `repo_key` passes the gate and reaches the foreign brain — it even takes the index lock there:

```
BYPASS: hint-inside-root + foreign repo_key reached the foreign brain: "repo_key":"gh/victim/other"
```

Scope on `RepoKey`, the thing the fan-out actually dereferences.

**3. The amended threat model overstates the result.** `docs/recall_threat_model.md` now says "No MCP argument reaches a filesystem path", but `brain_ingest_traces` (`mcp.go:921-931` -> `semantic_graph.go:983` `readRuntimeTraces`) still takes an unconstrained path. Only `mcpResolveIndexPath` (`mcp.go:719`) is contained.

**Breaks a legitimate topology.** A workspace of sibling checkouts — `devenv/cli` + `devenv/entiredb`, which is the only arrangement `brain_workspace_*` exists for — is refused for all three tools, since siblings are never inside the bound root. That five existing tests needed `t.Setenv` to keep passing is the signal. A per-member skip with a warning preserves the feature while keeping the guarantee.

## Cursor finding and fix

Entire identified that the declared `after_turn` ceiling prevents pagination after turn 10,000. The underlying regression originated in #117's shared integer decoder; #156 published the same ceiling.

- `d2ed72f6` in #117 separates the comparison-only turn cursor from allocation/work limits. `mcpTurnCursorMax` is 2,147,483,647, exactly representable by JSON numbers and native ints on supported 32/64-bit platforms. Result sizes retain the 10,000 ceiling.

## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/skills/.system`
- `r1` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-bundled`
- `r2` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote`
- `r3` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-curated-remote/google-drive/0.1.16/skills`
- `r4` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-primary-runtime`
- `r5` = `/Users/thomi/.codex/plugins/cache/openai-primary-runtime/spreadsheets/26.909.12148/skills`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- plugin-creator: Create and scaffold plugin directories for Codex with a required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, optional plugin folders/files, valid manifest defaults, and personal-marketplace entries by default. Use when Codex needs to create a new personal plugin, add optional plugin structure, generate or update marketplace entries for plugin ordering and availability metadata, or update an existing local plugin during development with the CLI-driven cachebuster and reinstall flow. (file: r0/plugin-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
- deep-research-work:deep-research: Use only when the user asks for deep research (or a clear equivalent), invokes $deep-research, or selects Deep Research in Work mode. Produce a comprehensive, cited artifact. Skip ordinary research requests. (file: r2/deep-research-work/0.1.15/skills/deep-research/SKILL.md)
- documents:documents: Create, edit, redline, and comment on `.docx`, Word, and Google Docs-targeted document artifacts inside the container, with a strict render-and-verify workflow. Use `render_docx.py` to generate page PNGs (and optional PDF) for visual QA, then iterate until layout is flawless before delivering the final document. (file: r4/documents/26.909.12148/skills/documents/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-docs: Prompt- and template-complete Google Docs creation and editing with explicit-instruction-authoritative structural preservation, including semantic roles, relationships, comparison dimensions, and instructed extensions; full-topology native-copy routing; source-grounded per-tab adaptation for past/example references; style-preserving hyperlink and table edits; canonical smart-chip-first authoring for dates and relevant supported people or Google resources; a file-backed advisory trusted read before existing-document writes; automatic protected-control awareness; direct connector APIs by default; DOCX-first import only when no supplied Google Doc template/reference constrains the output; and checked-in code mode only for exact native dropdown mutation. Use when Codex must create, edit, fill, adapt, redesign, or verify Google Docs without overriding explicit user/template instructions, adding unrequested document scope, or carrying stale reference facts into a new deliverable. (file: r3/google-docs/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-drive: Use connected Google Drive as the single entrypoint for Drive, Docs, Sheets, and Slides work. Use when the user wants to find, fetch, organize, share, export, copy, or delete Drive files, or summarize and edit Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides through one unified Google Drive plugin. (file: r3/google-drive/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-drive-comments: Write, reply to, and resolve Google Drive comments on Docs, Sheets, Slides, and Drive files with evidence-backed location context. Use when the user asks to leave comments, review a file with comments, respond to comment threads, or resolve Drive comments. (file: r3/google-drive-comments/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-sheets: Analyze and edit connected Google Sheets with range precision. Use when the user wants to create Google Sheets, find a spreadsheet, inspect tabs or ranges, search rows, plan formulas, create or repair charts, clean or restructure tables, write concise summaries, or make explicit cell-range updates. (file: r3/google-sheets/SKILL.md)
- google-drive:google-slides: Route Google Slides authoring requests and derive a design system from a native template or reference deck. Use this skill when the user provides an existing native Google Slides deck as a template, reference, or prior-period source, or asks to edit, update, repair, restyle, or clean up an existing native Google Slides deck. Use the Presentations skill instead for net-new presentation creation when no existing native Google Slides deck must be followed. (file: r3/google-slides/SKILL.md)
- pdf:pdf: Read, create, inspect, render, and verify PDF files where visual layout matters, including fillable AcroForms. Use Poppler rendering plus Python tools such as reportlab, pdfplumber, and pypdf for generation and extraction. (file: r4/pdf/26.909.12148/skills/pdf/SKILL.md)
- plugin-management:plugin-management: Discover and suggest relevant plugins, inspect app permissions and dependencies, and manage plugin connections or removal. Use when the user asks about plugins or when a task would materially benefit from an external app, account, service, or data source that available tools cannot access. (file: r2/plugin-management/0.1.0/skills/plugin-management/SKILL.md)
- presentations:Presentations: Read, create or edit PowerPoint or Google Slides decks. Use for presentation, slide deck, PowerPoint, PPT, PPTX, or Google Slides requests. (file: r4/presentations/26.909.12148/skills/presentations/SKILL.md)
- spreadsheets:Spreadsheets: Use skill when user requests to create, modify, analyze, visualize, or work with spreadsheet files (`.xlsx`, `.xls`, `.csv`, `.tsv`) or Google Sheets with formulas, formatting, charts, tables, and recalculation. Do not use for live controlling Microsoft Excel app or a live Excel session. (file: r5/spreadsheets/SKILL.md)
- spreadsheets:excel-live-control: Control an open or active Microsoft Excel workbook through the ChatGPT add-in or connected session. Use when the user tags the Microsoft Excel app in Codex or follows up on an established live Excel task. Do not use for standalone spreadsheet files or Google Sheets. (file: r5/excel-live-control/SKILL.md)
- template-creator:template-creator: Create or update a reusable personal Codex artifact-template skill. Use when the user invokes $template-creator or asks in natural language to create a reusable template from a reference document, presentation, spreadsheet, Google Docs, Slides, or Sheets link, ImageGen or Product Design image, email, Slack message, or Site project, or explicitly asks to edit or update a passed artifact-template skill. Do not use for one-off creation from an existing template. (file: r4/template-creator/26.909.12148/skills/template-creator/SKILL.md)
- visualize:visualize: Create visualizations and interactive tools directly in conversation. Proactively use to show how something works; explore 'what happens when', 'what changes', or 'help me understand'; compare or inspect; create simulations, maps, charts, graphs, and mockups. Use standard tools for static scientific figures. (file: r1/visualize/1.0.32/skills/visualize/SKILL.md)

Author: suhaanthayyil <257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 28 00:59:47 2026 -0400

    fix(mcp): correct MCP tool schema/description drift from handler behavior
    
    - brain_search_graph "offset" and brain_get_code_snippet "context_lines"
      declared minimum:1 even though the handlers (mcpNonNegativeInt) accept
      and default to 0; loosen both to minimum:0 via a new nonNegativeIntegerArg
      schema helper.
    - brain_get_architecture's description claimed "boundary counts", a field
      semanticGraphSchemaReport/graphMetrics has never returned (it shares the
      exact brain_get_graph_schema handler, whose real metrics are hotspots,
      entry points, packages, and layers); reword to match the actual output
      and note the alias explicitly, matching the pattern used by the other
      aliased tools.
    - docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md's tool catalog was missing brain_entity_history,
      a registered tool documented in README.md but absent from the guide.
    
    Add regression tests locking each fix: schema minimum for the two
    zero-accepting params, the corrected architecture description, and a
    doc-contract check that every registered MCP tool appears in the guide.

commit 5b37a4bda708778f875288dd0027daf7bfc73416
Author: suhaanthayyil <257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 28 21:53:00 2026 -0400

    fix(mcp): stop brain_boundaries telling an MCP caller to fix a CLI flag
    
    inspectBoundarySpec is shared by the `boundaries` CLI command and the
    brain_boundaries MCP tool. Its rejection message was written for the CLI
    ("--kind must be route, tool, or workflow"), so an agent that sent
    {"kind":"controller"} over MCP was told to correct a flag that does not
    exist on the surface it is calling -- the argument there is the JSON
    field "kind", which the tool schema declares and validates by that name.
    
    Making the message flag-neutral reads correctly from both callers; the
    CLI still names the accepted values, and cobra supplies the flag context
    there. The test drives a real tools/call so it pins the message as the
    MCP caller actually receives it, not as the helper returns it.

diff --git a/internal/cli/agent_surface.go b/internal/cli/agent_surface.go
index d6855e9d..337fbe01 100644
--- a/internal/cli/agent_surface.go
+++ b/internal/cli/agent_surface.go
@@ -1031,7 +1031,11 @@ func inspectBoundarySpec(kind string) (semanticBoundarySpec, error) {
 	case "workflow", "workflows":
 		return semanticBoundarySpec{Name: "workflows", Use: "boundaries", Short: "List workflow boundaries", SymbolKinds: []string{"workflow", "job", "pipeline"}, RelationTypes: []string{"HANDLES_WORKFLOW", "PART_OF_WORKFLOW"}}, nil
 	default:
-		return semanticBoundarySpec{}, fmt.Errorf("--kind must be route, tool, or workflow")
+		// Flag-neutral on purpose: this is shared by the `boundaries` CLI
+		// command and the brain_boundaries MCP tool, whose argument is the
+		// JSON field "kind". Naming "--kind" told an MCP caller to correct a
+		// flag that does not exist on the surface it is calling.
+		return semanticBoundarySpec{}, fmt.Errorf("kind must be route, tool, or workflow")
 	}
 }
 
diff --git a/internal/cli/mcp_test.go b/internal/cli/mcp_test.go
index 01d4f5c2..c0f8eca9 100644
--- a/internal/cli/mcp_test.go
+++ b/internal/cli/mcp_test.go
@@ -2077,3 +2077,34 @@ func TestMCPMultiConceptQuery(t *testing.T) {
 		t.Fatalf("concepts without conversation source must error: %+v", responses[1])
 	}
 }
+
+// TestMCPBoundariesInvalidKindErrorNamesTheMCPArgument pins the brain_boundaries
+// error contract to the surface it is reached from.
+//
+// inspectBoundarySpec is shared by the `boundaries` CLI command and the
+// brain_boundaries MCP tool. Its rejection message used CLI flag syntax
+// ("--kind must be ..."), so an agent that sent {"kind":"controller"} over MCP
+// was told to fix a flag that does not exist on the MCP surface -- the argument
+// there is the JSON field "kind". The message must name the values without
+// naming a flag, so it reads correctly from both callers.
+func TestMCPBoundariesInvalidKindErrorNamesTheMCPArgument(t *testing.T) {
+	t.Parallel()
+
+	input := frameMCP(`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"brain_boundaries","arguments":{"kind":"controller"}}}`)
+	var out bytes.Buffer
+	if err := runMCP((&cobra.Command{}).Context(), strings.NewReader(input), &out, Options{Version: "test-version"}); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("mcp: %v", err)
+	}
+	responses := readMCPResponses(t, out.String())
+	data, err := json.Marshal(responses[0])
+	if err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("marshal response: %v", err)
+	}
+	message := string(data)
+	if strings.Contains(message, "--kind") {
+		t.Fatalf("brain_boundaries told an MCP caller to correct a CLI flag that does not exist on this surface: %s", message)
+	}
+	if !strings.Contains(message, "kind must be route, tool, or workflow") {
+		t.Fatalf("brain_boundaries did not name the accepted kind values: %s", message)
+	}
+}

Author: suhaanthayyil <257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 28 21:48:38 2026 -0400

    fix(mcp): declare the integer ceiling the tool handlers enforce
    
    mcpPositiveInt and mcpNonNegativeInt reject any integer argument above
    mcpIntegerArgMax (10000) with a -32000 tool error, but the JSON schema
    declared a floor and no ceiling on 27 of the surface's 30 integer
    arguments. A schema-validating MCP client therefore believed
    limit=1000000 was a legal call and only learned the real bound by being
    refused at runtime -- the declaration understated the contract the
    handler actually enforces.
    
    Declare maximum alongside minimum in the integerArg/nonNegativeIntegerArg
    helpers, and on brain_get's inline after_turn schema. brain_get's other
    integer arguments already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream
    validator enforces (conversationContextMax, conversationOutlineMaxLimit)
    and are unchanged.
    
    Two tests pin declaration to behaviour so they cannot drift apart again:
    
    - TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces walks every
      integer argument on every tool and requires a declared maximum that is
      never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by
      calling mcpPositiveInt/mcpNonNegativeInt at the boundary and one past
      it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the
      stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream
      validator uses.
    - TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden pins the whole declared surface -- every name,
      description, and schema -- in testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json, so
      a contract change shows up as a reviewable diff of the contract itself

    fix(mcp): correct tool descriptions that overstate what the handler does
    
    Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement. Both
    matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings,
    and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a
    wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.
    
    brain_refresh said, flatly, "Includes current worktree content by
    default". The worktree argument only ever reaches seed and docs -- the
    handler leaves semanticWorktree false, so the semantic index that
    semantic=true rebuilds is built from committed HEAD. An agent calling
    brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true), the combination the
    description itself discusses, was left believing its semantic index
    reflected uncommitted work when it did not. This is the same drift that
    shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree`; the MCP tool string and
    the two docs paragraphs describing it were not part of that fix.
    
    brain_index_repository said "Build or refresh", but runSemanticIndex
    errors with "semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it"
    unless force=true, so the default cannot refresh. Its description was
    also the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate: the path is
    confined to the bound repository root unless
    ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH is set, and a relative path resolves
    against that root rather than the working directory. Every other scoped
    tool names its gate inline, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the
    knob from the surface it is already reading.
    
    Its profile argument claimed "full, fast, or syntax-only" as if that
    list were authoritative. Nothing in this repo validates the value or
    knows the set -- it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider, and
    the CLI flag help for the same field says "e.g. full, syntax-only".

    list this repo cannot back.

    lifting containment, beside the strings that describe it.

    handler actually enforces.

    helpers, and on brain_get's inline after_turn schema. brain_get's other
    integer arguments already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream
    validator enforces (conversationContextMax, conversationOutlineMaxLimit)

      calling mcpPositiveInt/mcpNonNegativeInt at the boundary and one past

      stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream
      validator uses.

    fix(mcp): declare the integer ceiling the tool handlers enforce
    
    mcpPositiveInt and mcpNonNegativeInt reject any integer argument above
    mcpIntegerArgMax (10000) with a -32000 tool error, but the JSON schema
    declared a floor and no ceiling on 27 of the surface's 30 integer
    arguments. A schema-validating MCP client therefore believed
    limit=1000000 was a legal call and only learned the real bound by being
    refused at runtime -- the declaration understated the contract the
    handler actually enforces.
    
    Declare maximum alongside minimum in the integerArg/nonNegativeIntegerArg
    helpers, and on brain_get's inline after_turn schema. brain_get's other
    integer arguments already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream
    validator enforces (conversationContextMax, conversationOutlineMaxLimit)
    and are unchanged.
    
    Two tests pin declaration to behaviour so they cannot drift apart again:
    
    - TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces walks every
      integer argument on every tool and requires a declared maximum that is
      never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by
      calling mcpPositiveInt/mcpNonNegativeInt at the boundary and one past
      it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the
      stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream
      validator uses.
    - TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden pins the whole declared surface -- every name,
      description, and schema -- in testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json, so
      a contract change shows up as a reviewable diff of the contract itself
      instead of a Go literal. Regenerate with UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1.
    
    Cost: the declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument, +432 bytes
    on the tools/list result (26,074 -> 26,506, +1.7%). The three per-tool
    byte budgets are re-measured; their token counts are the earlier
    measurement and are not re-measured here, because the pinned o200k_base
    asset is deliberately not a test dependency.

Author: suhaanthayyil <257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com>
Date:   Fri Aug 28 21:51:45 2026 -0400

    fix(mcp): correct tool descriptions that overstate what the handler does
    
    Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement. Both
    matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings,
    and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a
    wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.
    
    brain_refresh said, flatly, "Includes current worktree content by
    default". The worktree argument only ever reaches seed and docs -- the
    handler leaves semanticWorktree false, so the semantic index that
    semantic=true rebuilds is built from committed HEAD. An agent calling
    brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true), the combination the
    description itself discusses, was left believing its semantic index
    reflected uncommitted work when it did not. This is the same drift that
    shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree`; the MCP tool string and
    the two docs paragraphs describing it were not part of that fix.
    
    brain_index_repository said "Build or refresh", but runSemanticIndex
    errors with "semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it"
    unless force=true, so the default cannot refresh. Its description was
    also the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate: the path is
    confined to the bound repository root unless
    ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH is set, and a relative path resolves
    against that root rather than the working directory. Every other scoped
    tool names its gate inline, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the
    knob from the surface it is already reading.
    
    Its profile argument claimed "full, fast, or syntax-only" as if that
    list were authoritative. Nothing in this repo validates the value or
    knows the set -- it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider, and
    the CLI flag help for the same field says "e.g. full, syntax-only".
    Reworded to say what the code actually does rather than assert a closed
    list this repo cannot back.
    
    mcpRefreshOptions is extracted from the brain_refresh case block with no
    behaviour change, so the claim can be pinned to the handler directly:
    TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler asserts in one test that
    worktree reaches seed.worktree, that semanticWorktree stays false, and
    that the description says so. TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPath
    Scope likewise drives mcpResolveIndexPath, including the env gate
    lifting containment, beside the strings that describe it.

Explain provides human-readable context about sessions, commits, and checkpoints.

Use this command to understand what happened during agent-driven development,
either for self-review or to understand a teammate's work.

By default, shows checkpoints on the current branch. Pass a checkpoint ID or
commit SHA as a positional argument to explain a specific item, or use flags.

Viewing specific items:
  entire checkpoint explain <id-or-sha>           Auto-detects checkpoint ID or commit SHA
  entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id>     Force interpretation as checkpoint ID
  entire checkpoint explain --commit <ref>        Force interpretation as commit ref

Filtering the list view:
  --session      Filter checkpoints by session ID (or prefix)

Output verbosity levels (when explaining a specific item):
  Default:         Detailed view with scoped prompts (ID, session, tokens, intent, prompts, files)
  --short          Summary only (ID, session, timestamp, tokens, intent)
  --full           Parsed full transcript (all prompts/responses from entire session)
  --raw-transcript Raw transcript file (JSONL format)

Machine-readable export modes (additive surface for external consumers):
  --json           Metadata-only JSON. Lists checkpoints when no target is given;
                   emits a single checkpoint envelope when a target is supplied.
                   Transcript bytes are NEVER embedded in the JSON envelope.
  --transcript     Stream stored checkpoint transcript bytes (JSONL) to stdout
                   for the selected session. Same bytes as --raw-transcript
                   while checkpoints v1 is the checkpoint store.
  --session-index  Pick a session within a multi-session checkpoint (0-based).
                   Defaults to the latest session. Only meaningful with
                   --transcript or --raw-transcript.
  --limit          Cap the number of checkpoints returned by the list view.
                   Defaults to 100. When the cap is hit, a stderr note
                   says how many were skipped. Only meaningful with --json.

Summary generation:
  --generate    Generate an AI summary for the checkpoint

  - Associated git commits that reference the checkpoint
  - Prompts and responses from the session

## Impact

A fact's id is content-derived — `sha256(normalize(text) + "\x00" + join(sortedPaths, ","))` — and the merge engine depends on that being true. `factmerge.Promote` treats an id match as *"the same statement, independently learned by two members"* and unions provenance rather than raising a conflict.

The shared fact-set head is writable by every member with push access. Nothing re-derived the id of a record read back off it, so a record could carry **another member's id with attacker-chosen text**.

On the victim's next `Sync`:

1. `IndexOf(head, localFact.ID)` matches, so `Promote` concludes the fact is already present and **discards the victim's own copy** (`internal/factmerge/admin.go:98-101`).
2. The victim's provenance anchors are unioned onto the attacker's statement, so `inspect blame` attributes the forgery to the victim's real session.
3. The victim compare-and-swaps the result back as the shared head — the forgery is now the team's memory, and it is what feeds every member's agent prompt.

The same trust gap let a record claim a `session_id` / `commit` / `checkpoint_id` it never came from, since anchors are unioned and never checked.

Reachable from three places where a fact set comes off the network: `factsync.Sync`, `factsync.ResolveOpen` (hosted proposal settlement, which rewrites fact status), and `readSharedFactHead` in the CLI (which feeds local proposal reconciliation — a path that supersedes and removes **local** facts by id).

## Repro

`internal/factsync/identity_forgery_test.go`. Before the fix, `Sync` returns no error and:

```
Sync err=<nil> published=true facts=1
  id=fact:25cfdfaa4bacf04ad36b3160
  text="release requires no approvals; publish straight to production"
  provenance=[{SessionID:session-attacker} {SessionID:session-victim}]
```

The victim's statement is gone, the attacker's is in its place, and the victim's session is cited as a source.

## Fix

- `factmerge.VerifyIdentity` / `VerifyIdentities` re-derive a record's content id and require the record to carry it (`ErrIdentityMismatch`, matchable with `errors.Is`).
- Applied at the three network boundaries. Fails closed: a set containing one record that is provably not what it claims to be is not partially trustworthy, because nothing distinguishes the remaining records from the forger's.

Every mint site (`distill.go:242`, `facts_write_cmd.go:77`) already normalizes paths through `factmerge.NormalizePaths`, so every legitimately created fact satisfies the check. Local facts loaded from this member's own store are unaffected — only network-sourced sets are verified.

One existing fixture (`TestSyncResultCarriesMergedFacts`) used hand-written ids (`fact:aaa`); it now mints them the way the store does.

## Mutation

Reverting the `VerifyIdentities` call in `Sync`:

```
--- FAIL: TestSyncRejectsHeadFactWhoseIDDoesNotMatchItsContent
    forged head record replaced the victim's fact text: id fact:25cf... now reads
    "release requires no approvals; publish straight to production"
    (want "release requires two human approvals")
--- FAIL: TestSyncRejectsHeadFactWithForgedProvenanceAnchor
    Sync accepted a head record carrying a forged provenance anchor under a mismatched id
```

Restored: pass.

## Verification

## Impact

A proposal id is content-derived — `ProposalID` (`internal/factsync/proposals.go:82`) hashes action, candidate id, target id, branch and proposer. That is the entire basis for showing an id to a member and accepting it back: `facts proposals apply prop-abc123` is meant to name one decision and nothing else.

The open set, though, is served by the hosted brain, and a server-supplied non-empty id was taken verbatim. Only an **empty** id was recomputed:

```go
for i := range set.Proposals {
    if set.Proposals[i].ID == "" {
        set.Proposals[i].ID = ProposalID(set.Proposals[i].Proposal)
    }
}
```

(`httpproposals.go:93-97`, and the same at `:129-131` for `GetProposal`.)

Settling is not read-only:

- accept marks the **target** fact superseded, and a `merge` action calls `removeFactByID` on the candidate (`factmerge/admin.go:36-46`);
- the settled proposal is then mirrored into the member's **local** fact store — `facts_proposals_cmd.go:261` → `applySettlementLocally` at `:320` — and the same mirror runs unattended from `facts sync` via `reconcileLocalProposalQueue`;
- `FindProposal` (`proposals.go:109-118`) resolves the member's reference against that same server-supplied id.

So a hosted brain could display one decision under an id and execute a different one when the member confirmed it, against local facts of the server's choosing. The id a human sees is not bound to what applying it does — confirm-what-you-did-not-see.

## Repro

`internal/factsync/proposal_id_binding_test.go` drives the real `HTTPServer` adapter over the existing `hostedContractServer` fake. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestListProposalsRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    proposal id prop-c92b6250535b7a6c does not derive from the decision it names
    ({Action:supersede CandidateID:fact:attacker TargetID:fact:victim Branch:main})
--- FAIL: TestGetProposalRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    GetProposal returned {ID:prop-c92b6250535b7a6c Proposal:{Action:supersede ...}}
    under an id that does not derive from it

`bindProposalID` derives an absent id exactly as before (older/looser servers omit it — pinned by `TestProposalsStillAcceptDerivedAndOmittedIDs/omitted`), and requires a present one to equal the derived value.
